blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: The centre of gravity of an object, the moment of a force about a point, couples, and the torque of a couple.

blocks.heading: Centre of gravity
blocks.text: The weight of an object is really the pull of the Earth on every part of it, part by part. In force and moment calculations the whole of that weight may be taken to act at a single point, called the centre of gravity of the object. The centre of gravity is the point where the moments of the weights of all the parts balance. For a uniform object of symmetrical shape, such as a metre rule or a solid ball, the centre of gravity sits at the geometric centre of the object. For some objects it lies outside the material altogether: the centre of gravity of a uniform ring is at its centre, in the empty space, and the centre of gravity of a boomerang lies between its arms.

blocks.heading: Why one point is enough
blocks.text: Taking the whole weight as one force acting at the centre of gravity gives the same turning effect as adding up the effect of the weight of each part separately. That is what makes the substitution valid: the centre of gravity is defined as the point where the separate moments of the parts balance, so the single force there reproduces the total turning effect about a pivot. When a uniform plank balances on a fulcrum placed directly under its centre of gravity, the clockwise and anticlockwise moments of its parts match, and it sits level. The same shortcut lets a crane driver treat a loaded container as one force acting at one point.

blocks.heading: Moment of a force
blocks.text: Forces can turn things as well as push them. The moment of a force about a point is the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force. In symbols, moment = Fd, where F is the force in newtons (N) and d is the perpendicular distance in metres (m) from the point to the line of action of the force. The unit of moment is the newton metre, written N m. The distance must be measured at right angles to the force: imagine dropping a line from the point at 90° to the direction in which the force acts, and taking that line's length. A force whose line of action passes straight through the point has a perpendicular distance of zero, so its moment about that point is zero. A push directed straight through a hinge does not swing the door, however hard it is applied.

blocks.heading: A force at an angle
blocks.text: A force does not need to act at right angles to the thing it turns. When a force acts at an angle to a lever, only its component at right angles to the lever does the turning. The moment about the pivot is then F × d × sin θ, where F is the force in newtons, θ is the angle between the force and the lever, and d is the distance along the lever from the pivot to the point where the force is applied. There are two equivalent routes to the same answer: multiply the force by the component of the distance perpendicular to it, or multiply the perpendicular component of the force by the distance along the lever. A longer lever gives a larger moment for the same force, which is why a long spanner shifts a stubborn wheel nut where a short one does not.

blocks.heading: Worked example: a wheel spanner
blocks.text: A mechanic changes a wheel on a minibus taxi outside Otjiwarongo. A wheel nut needs a moment of 45 N m to loosen it. Her spanner reaches 0.30 m from the nut to her hand, and she pushes at right angles to it with a force of 150 N. The moment is moment = Fd = 150 N × 0.30 m = 45 N m, which matches what the nut needs, so it turns. If she pushes along the spanner instead, at 0° to its length, the component at right angles to the spanner is zero, so the moment is zero however hard she pushes. At 40° to the spanner the same 150 N gives only 150 N × 0.30 m × sin 40°, which is about 29 N m: too little. Distance perpendicular to the force, and nothing else, is what counts.

blocks.heading: Couples
blocks.text: Some arrangements of forces are built to turn things and to do nothing else. A couple is a pair of forces that are equal in size, opposite in direction and parallel, and whose lines of action do not coincide. Because the two forces are equal and opposite, they add to zero as vectors: a couple produces no resultant force at all, and it acts to produce rotation only. Turning a car's steering wheel with two hands makes a couple: one hand pushes one side of the rim up and the other pulls the opposite side down, with forces of equal size. The wheel is not pushed sideways, because the two forces cancel as a push; it is turned, because they do not cancel as a turning effect.

blocks.heading: A couple turns without pushing
blocks.text: The total moment of a couple comes out the same whatever point is chosen as the pivot, which is what makes it a property of the pair of forces rather than of any particular point. Take two forces of size F whose lines of action are a perpendicular distance s apart. About a point on the line of action of one force, that force has zero moment and the other acts at a distance s, giving a total moment Fs. About a point midway between them, each force acts at a distance of s/2 and the two moments point the same way, giving F × s/2 twice, which is Fs again. About any other point the two individual moments change, but their sum stays Fs. A couple is pure turning effect, free of any push.

blocks.heading: Torque of a couple
blocks.text: The torque of a couple is one of the forces multiplied by the perpendicular distance between the two lines of action. In symbols, torque = Fs, where F is one of the forces in newtons and s is the perpendicular distance between the forces in metres. Like a moment, torque is measured in newton metres (N m). The word torque belongs to a pair of forces: for a single force we speak of its moment about a chosen point. Because the total moment of a couple is the same about a point, the torque of a couple can be stated without naming a pivot at all.

blocks.heading: Worked example: a steering wheel
blocks.text: A driver turns a minibus steering wheel of diameter 0.42 m, gripping opposite points of the rim. Each hand applies a force of 11 N tangentially to the rim, one up and one down, so the hands form a couple. The perpendicular distance between the two lines of action is the diameter, 0.42 m. Torque = Fs = 11 N × 0.42 m = 4.62 N m, so the torque is 4.6 N m to two significant figures. Checking the same answer the longer way, about the centre of the wheel: each force has a moment of 11 N × 0.21 m = 2.31 N m in the same sense, and the two add to 4.62 N m. Either route gives the same torque, as it must, because the moment of a couple does not depend on the point chosen.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: Moments, couples and torque are the tools of the next sub-topic, 4.2, where the principle of moments balances a beam or a ladder in equilibrium. Torque returns in topic 6, where the twisting of a wire is described the same way. Centre of gravity belongs with weight, W = mg, from topic 3, and it matters wherever the stability of a vehicle or a stack is discussed.
